quote: Man kann von der Invariantentheorie der binären Formen ganz loslösen das Problem der Aufstellung aller ganzen rationalen Funk- tionen, welche bei Anwendung einer einzi- gen linearen ganzzahligen Substitution d.h. Aufstellung de[-sjenigen-] vollen Systems solcher Invarianten.
english: One can completely detach from the invariant theory of binary forms the problem of determining all integral rational functions which [remain unchanged] under application of a single linear integral substitution, i.e. determining the full system of such invariants.
topic: Hilbert proposes reducing a set of conditions by considering moduli of the form (φ, ψ, (x−a)^λ(y−b)^μ), then remarks that finding all integral rational functions invariant under a single integral linear substitution can be separated from binary invariant theory, and that invariance under infinitely many substitutions essentially yields only semi-invariants.

triage.modern_statement: Take a single matrix g in GL_n(Z) (or GL_n(K), char K = 0) acting linearly on the polynomial ring K[x_1,...,x_n]. Determine the invariant ring K[x]^g = {f : f(gx) = f(x)}. In particular, is it finitely generated, and what is an explicit complete ('full') system of generators? If g has finite order, this is the invariant theory of a finite cyclic group. If g has infinite order, the invariants of g are the invariants of its Zariski closure. When g is unipotent, they are the kernel of the linear locally nilpotent ('Weitzenböck') derivation log(g). This is the G_a-invariant setting, which is closely tied to semi-invariants and covariants of binary forms. That fits Hilbert's remark that invariance under infinitely many substitutions essentially gives only semi-invariants.
triage.answered_by: The key case, finite generation of the invariants of a single unipotent linear substitution, is the classical theorem of R. Weitzenböck (1932). C. S. Seshadri later gave a modern proof. The invariant ring of a single unipotent transformation is the same as the algebra of constants of the corresponding Weitzenböck derivation. Finding explicit generating systems is still worked on case by case, for example by Drensky and coauthors. The finite-order case falls under the general finiteness theorems for finite groups (Hilbert/Noether), but my searches did not return a source for that part.

evidence.claim: Weitzenböck's classical theorem (1932) says that the algebra of constants of a linear locally nilpotent derivation (Weitzenböck derivation) is finitely generated.
The algebra of constants K[X_d]^δ is the same as the algebra of invariants of a single unipotent transformation, and it is finitely generated.
By Weitzenböck's theorem, the algebra of invariants K[X]^g of a single unipotent transformation g in GL_m(K) is finitely generated. Seshadri gave a proof in modern language.
Constants of Weitzenböck derivations and invariants of unipotent transformations are still being studied, including generalizations to relatively free algebras (Drensky et al.).

triage.why: Hilbert's note asks for the full invariant system of a single linear integral substitution, separated from binary invariant theory. In modern terms, this is the invariant ring of a cyclic linear group. The hard, infinite-order (unipotent) case was settled for finite generation by Weitzenböck in 1932, and Seshadri later gave a modern proof. The sources directly support this and also show that the topic is still active: the open work is computing explicit generators and generalizing to noncommutative or relatively free algebras. The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. I cannot confirm from sources that Weitzenböck was answering Hilbert's diary note directly, and I found no source citation for the finite-order case. The mixed semisimple-times-unipotent case follows by standard reductions, but I did not verify that with a source. That is why confidence is medium, not high.
